units.title: Unit 57 — Possession and giving
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 120–121 (PDF pages 121–122).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish possessions, personal belongings, property and the different meanings of estate, including countability.
Use the correct terms for business owners, landlords, landladies, tenants and inheritance.
Choose the appropriate verb and preposition patterns for providing, donating, sponsoring, allocating and presenting.
Understand the different meanings of giving phrasal verbs such as hand over, hand down and give away.

sectionsChecked: A: Possessions, belongings, estate, housing estate and countable/uncountable property
B: Proprietor, owner, landlord, landlady, tenant and inheritance
C: Provision, supply, presentation, support, charity and allocation
D: Phrasal verbs for giving and transfer

items.pt: bens; pertences; tudo o que alguém possui
items.example: After years of travelling, Marta decided to sell most of her possessions.
items.note: Everything a person owns, including possessions of different kinds.

items.example: Please collect your belongings before leaving the changing room.
items.note: Always plural; usually refers to personal items such as clothes, bags and cameras.

items.pt: grande propriedade rural; terras com construções
items.example: The family owns a large estate surrounded by farmland.
items.note: A single large area of privately owned land, often with buildings.

items.pt: patrimônio deixado por alguém após a morte; espólio
items.example: The solicitor estimated her estate before distributing the inheritance.
items.note: Here estate means a person's total wealth and assets when they die.

items.pt: conjunto habitacional; bairro de habitações planejadas
items.example: A new housing estate was built near the railway station.
items.note: A residential area of many houses or flats developed together; British English.

items.pt: bens imóveis; propriedade imobiliária em geral
items.example: Property has become expensive in the city centre.
items.note: Uncountable when referring generally to land and buildings as things owned.

items.example: The agency advertised a property close to the university.
items.note: Countable for an individual building or piece of land.

items.example: Several properties on the street have recently been renovated.
items.note: Plural of a property, referring to separate buildings or pieces of land.

items.example: The proprietor of the café welcomed the new customers.
items.note: Formal word for the owner of a shop, restaurant or business.

items.example: The owner decided to close the shop for repairs.
items.note: More common and less formal than proprietor.

items.example: Our landlord arranged for the broken heating system to be repaired.
items.note: A male person, or any person when gender is unspecified, who rents a property to tenants.

items.example: The landlady inspected the flat after the tenants moved out.
items.note: A female owner who rents a property to others.

items.example: The tenant contacted the agency about a leak in the bathroom.
items.note: Someone who rents accommodation or land from an owner.

items.example: Their rent increased when the contract was renewed.
items.note: A noun for the money paid to use property; rent is also a verb.

items.example: The owner promised not to put the rent up during the first year.
items.note: British English phrasal pattern meaning increase the rent.

items.example: He inherited a small cottage from his grandfather.
items.note: Receive property, money or other things after someone's death.

items.example: The council provides clean drinking water for local residents.
items.note: Provide something for someone; also provide someone with something.

items.example: The organisers provided every volunteer with safety equipment.
items.note: Provide someone with something, or provide something for someone.

items.example: A local company supplies the clinic with medical equipment.
items.note: Supply someone with something; often used for regular provision or commercial deliveries.

items.example: The farm supplies fresh vegetables to several restaurants.
items.note: May imply regular or commercial provision of goods; also a noun.

items.example: The principal presented the prize to the winning student.
items.note: Formal giving; also present someone with a prize or gift. This verb is pronounced /prɪˈzent/.

items.example: Her family supported her financially throughout her studies.
items.note: Provide financial or practical help; may also mean emotional support.

items.pt: atender às necessidades de; servir a
items.example: The school kitchen caters for around two hundred pupils each day.
items.note: Provide meals or services for a group; British English.

items.example: The retired teacher left money to a local animal charity.
items.note: In a will, leave something to someone or an institution after death.

items.example: She donated her old textbooks to the community library.
items.note: Often used for gifts of money or goods to charities and institutions.

items.pt: contribuir para; fazer uma contribuição a
items.example: The whole department contributed to the farewell gift.
items.note: Give money, time or effort towards a shared cause, project or fund.

items.example: Several colleagues sponsored him for a charity cycle ride.
items.note: Here: promise or give money to support a person taking part in a charity event.

items.example: The coordinator allocated a desk to each new researcher.
items.note: Officially assign a room, place, resource or amount to someone.

items.pt: entregar; transferir a posse ou responsabilidade
items.example: Please hand over the access card when your contract ends.
items.note: Give control, responsibility or an object to another person.

items.example: She found it difficult to let go of the guitar she had owned for years.
items.note: Can mean release physically or be unwilling to part with something valuable.

items.example: The instructor handed out worksheets before the class began.
items.note: Give individual items to members of a group; similar to give out.

items.example: Volunteers gave out water to runners at the finish line.
items.note: Here give out means distribute; not the unrelated sense of stop working.

items.example: We gave away the furniture we no longer needed.
items.note: Give something to another person without asking for payment.

items.pt: passar de geração em geração; transmitir como herança
items.example: The silver watch has been handed down through four generations.
items.note: Pass an object or tradition from an older generation to a younger one.

items.example: After the funeral, the siblings learnt that they had inherited a house.
items.note: A useful verb plus object collocation reinforced by the exercises.

items.pt: possuir imóveis; ser proprietário de bens imóveis
items.example: Many graduates find it difficult to own property in expensive cities.
items.note: Property here is uncountable and refers generally to real estate.

items.example: They decided to rent a flat rather than buy a house.
items.note: British English flat; renting gives the tenant use of a home without ownership.

items.example: Visitors can make a donation to the museum restoration fund.
items.note: Nominal form connected with donate, reinforced by the donation context.

units.title: Unit 58 — Movement and speed
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 122–123 (PDF pages 123–124).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe movement with precise natural collocations for vehicles, rivers, people and objects.
Contrast verbs of slow, fast, abrupt and repeated movement, including irregular past forms.
Distinguish the typical uses of speed, rate, pace and scientific velocity.
Use at with speed, rate and pace and distinguish fast, quick, rapid and swift.

sectionsChecked: A: Typical movement verbs and natural collocations
B: Fast and slow movement, including crawl, dawdle, tear, creep and cruise
C: Speed, rate, pace and velocity; common preposition mistake
Exercises 58.1–58.6, near-synonym guidance and the answer key

items.pt: mudar de casa; mudar de residência
items.example: We are planning to move house before the end of the year.
items.note: Move can mean change one's home or address, not just change physical position.

items.example: Delivery vehicles travel along country roads every morning.
items.note: Road vehicles travel or drive along roads; typical movement collocation.

items.example: She drives along the coast whenever the weather is good.
items.note: Drive refers to operating a road vehicle; past drove, past participle driven.

items.example: The freight train travels along rails through the valley.
items.note: Typical way to describe how trains move.

items.example: The ferry sails across the bay several times a day.
items.note: Boats and ships sail on rivers or across seas, including powered vessels.

items.example: A narrow river flows through the village.
items.note: Used especially for water and other liquids moving in a continuous stream.

items.example: A shallow stream runs through the orchard.
items.note: A river or stream can run through a town or area, like flow through.

items.example: The cyclist swerved to avoid a deep hole in the road.
items.note: Suddenly change direction to one side, often to avoid something.

items.pt: derivar; deslocar-se lentamente sem controle definido
items.example: Thin clouds drifted across the mountains.
items.note: Move slowly, often carried by wind or water, without a fixed course.

items.example: The curtains fluttered in the breeze through the open window.
items.note: Move lightly and repeatedly, often in air, like a flag or wings.

items.example: The leaves barely stirred on the windless afternoon.
items.note: Make a small movement; past stirred, not stired.

items.pt: balançar lentamente de um lado para o outro
items.example: The tall lamp posts swayed in the storm.
items.note: Move slowly back and forth or from side to side.

items.pt: para a frente e para trás; de um lado para outro
items.example: The suspended platform moved back and forth as workers climbed aboard.
items.note: Repeated movement in opposite directions; often with sway.

items.example: Traffic crawled through the tunnel during the roadworks.
items.note: Extremely slow movement; also used for babies and insects.

items.example: We need to leave now, so please don't dawdle on the way.
items.note: Move or act more slowly than necessary; often disapproving.

items.pt: disparar; correr ou avançar em alta velocidade
items.example: A motorbike tore along the narrow street despite the speed limit.
items.note: Informal, vivid expression for travelling very fast; tear has past form tore.

items.pt: passar disparado por; passar muito rapidamente
items.example: A racing car shot past the spectators in an instant.
items.note: Shoot past someone or something means move past extremely quickly.

items.example: I hurried to the station when I realised the train was leaving soon.
items.note: Move or act quickly because time is limited.

items.example: The passengers rushed towards the platform when boarding began.
items.note: Often suggests even greater urgency or sudden movement than hurry.

items.example: He crept along the corridor so he would not wake anyone.
items.note: Slow, careful or quiet movement; irregular past crept, not creeped.

items.example: After the long climb, the hikers plodded towards the campsite.
items.note: Slow, heavy movement, often showing tiredness or effort.

items.pt: deslocar-se a velocidade constante; voar em cruzeiro
items.example: The aircraft cruised steadily above the clouds.
items.note: Travel at a relatively constant speed, especially a vehicle or aircraft.

items.example: The train entered the tunnel at high speed.
items.note: Use at with speed, not with or in when expressing the manner of travel.

items.example: The engineer measured the speed of the conveyor belt.
items.note: General word for how fast something moves or changes.

items.example: The rate of production increased after the upgrade.
items.note: Often used for numerical or statistical changes, such as a rate of increase.

items.example: The lecture moved at a comfortable pace.
items.note: Expresses how fast or slow an activity feels as it progresses.

items.example: The students calculated the velocity of the falling object.
items.note: Technical and scientific term for the motion of an object.

items.example: We were making progress, although only at a slow pace.
items.note: Pace takes at, not in or with, when specifying a rate of progress.

items.example: The company's rate of growth slowed after its first year.
items.note: Common statistical collocation with rate of; not pace of for this sense.

items.example: The express train travels fast between the two cities.
items.note: Both adjective and adverb: a fast train and travel fast.

items.example: We took a quick break before starting the next experiment.
items.note: Adjective often used of short actions or quick responses; adverb is quickly.

items.example: The city has seen a rapid increase in housing costs.
items.note: Adjective common in relatively formal descriptions of increases or declines.

items.example: The safety team made a swift decision to stop the test.
items.note: Adjective often used with action, response, decision or reaction.

items.pt: pronto para responder; rápido em responder
items.example: The support team was quick to respond to the alarm.
items.note: Quick to plus infinitive describes prompt action; an exercise-related pattern.

items.pt: rápido em reagir; ágil para reagir
items.example: The operator was swift to react when the warning light came on.
items.note: Swift can take to plus an infinitive, describing decisive action.

items.example: The second test ran at a faster speed than the first.
items.note: The appropriate preposition with speed is at.

items.example: I drifted off to sleep while listening to the rain.
items.note: Figurative extension of drift, explicitly discussed in the unit's answer key.

items.pt: a mente divagar; os pensamentos se desviarem
items.example: During the long meeting, my thoughts drifted towards the weekend.
items.note: Figurative: thoughts move unintentionally to another subject.
